segments.text: Welcome to the daily Robotics News Digest, November 3rd, 2026.
We've got 18 updates, including breakthroughs in multi-vendor robot collaboration, the ROS Core release, and the exciting DG-4F introduction.
From Robotics & Automation News, "New ISO standard enables mobile robots from different vendors to work together".

This report details the publication of a new international standard designed to establish common communication and interoperability among industrial mobile robots from various vendors operating within the same facility.
The standard specifies the requirements for how robots, fleet managers, and associated equipment can exchange critical data including location, operational status, and tasking information.
This framework is intended to minimize path interference, enhance overall system efficiency, and promote market competition in the sector.
The standard also addresses communication protocols for interfacing with external systems such as enterprise resource planning tools and building automation systems.
Adoption of this standard is expected to create a more cohesive operational environment for industrial automation.
The development signals a step toward standardized industrial robotics integration across diverse supply chains.
From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: Intrinsic Core released: Open-source, ROS-compatible real-time control, motion planning and more".
This report details the release of Intrinsic Core, an open-source, ROS-compatible real-time control framework designed for industrial robotics.
The framework provides a hardware-agnostic runtime, SDK, and framework encompassing real-time control, motion planning, and grasp planning capabilities.
The release includes a pre-configured setup with simulation tools and a reference solution known as the Open Machine Tending Solution, or OMTS.
Community members are currently developing variations of OMTS, applying the framework to practical tasks such as object picking and insertion.
This development emphasizes a collaborative approach to practical industrial automation.
The open nature of Intrinsic Core establishes a new foundation for robotics development and real-time system integration.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, DG-4F!".
This segment reports on the assessment of Tesollo's four-finger robotic hand, which scored six out of ten overall.
The assessment indicated a higher capability for dexterity compared to grip strength within the framework used for evaluation.
The evaluation specifically noted that flexibility and strength require separate assessment depending on the handling requirements of the device.
The robotic hand is currently listed as in production with an advertised price of twelve thousand United States dollars from Tesollo in South Korea.
Buyers are advised to assess specific dexterity and force requirements rather than relying solely on the aggregate score provided.
This development suggests a focus on fine motor skills in robotic manipulation technologies moving forward.
From Humanoid.guide, Nvidia humanoid platforms rely on robot hands with China ties.

This report details how Nvidia's reference platforms utilize mechanical hands from Chinese startup Wuji and hands from Singapore-based Sharpa, indicating that robot training packages depend on specialized suppliers for body and manipulation hardware rather than a single manufacturer.

Practitioners have noted trade-offs among these hand selections concerning task performance, thermal behavior, and cost, framing hand choice as a balancing act against these practical constraints in humanoid development.
This modular hardware approach signifies a trend toward diversified supply chains in advanced robotics research.
Industry focus will remain on optimizing these component trade-offs for future humanoid system deployment.
From Robotics & Automation News, Tutor Intelligence raises seventy-five million dollars to scale robot workforce.

This report details a Series B funding round totaling one hundred seventeen million dollars led by Andreessen Horowitz, which will support the training of frontier robot foundation models and the deployment of robot workers named Sonny and Cassie.
The company operates by bridging the gap between robot capabilities and human capabilities through the use of real-world deployment data for training.

Tutor utilizes internet-connected robots operated by remote tutors to perform actual work within production environments, establishing a cycle that enhances robot intelligence, reduces cost, and facilitates wider workforce automation.
This development signals a focus on integrating real-world operational experience into advanced robotics training methodologies.
From Humanoids Daily, "Humanoid Robot Batteries Could Become an $850 Million Market by 2037, IDTechEx Forecasts".
This report details the projected market size for batteries powering humanoid robots, forecasting a total market value of eight hundred fifty million US dollars by the year two thousand thirty-seven.

The forecast is derived from an anticipated ten-year compound annual growth rate of thirty-four point two percent, factoring in both the demand for new robot batteries and the necessity for spare batteries in swapping systems.

The analysis incorporated performance metrics across various battery technologies assessed for industrial, commercial, and domestic humanoid applications, with consideration given to solutions that extend robot operational time through battery swapping.
This projection highlights the growing commercial viability of energy solutions within the humanoid robotics sector.
Attention should be directed toward advancements in energy density and swapping technology moving forward.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Opinion: What happens when the robot is wrong?".
This story examines the necessary procedures for experienced operators to challenge machine decisions to prevent errors from propagating.
Increased robot speed requires a clear process for human intervention to maintain safety.
Effective commissioning protocols must incorporate rehearsals involving false positives and conflicting instructions to assess human response and decision-making authority.
Systems must maintain exception records documenting operator challenges, evidence, and responses across shifts.
Successful system evaluation requires metrics assessing human-AI teaming alongside traditional performance measures.
This emphasizes the need for robust, documented human oversight in advanced automation systems.
From Robohub, "Muscle coordination can be mimicked by electric motors – it could lead to improved robots".

This story details research demonstrating that muscle-like coordination can be mimicked using electric motors, showing that muscle behavior emerges from the physical arrangement of motors and their shared mechanical structure rather than continuous programming.

Researchers constructed a physical model utilizing electric motors to simulate muscle coordination, revealing that motor-like behavior arises from the physical arrangement and shared mechanical structure of the motors, not from direct programming commands.

The setup demonstrated that motors can coordinate by briefly engaging a shared backbone, permitting the collective transmission of forces, establishing a principle of coordination without a central conductor.
This method suggests a pathway toward developing simpler and more adaptable designs for robotic systems.
This research indicates a direction toward creating more organic and adaptive robotic systems.
From The Robot Report, Churchill Capital XI shareholders approved a two point five billion dollar special purpose acquisition company transaction with Agility Robotics.
This action authorizes Agility Robotics to become a publicly traded company with the transaction anticipated to finalize on November fourth.
The funding secured is designated to support the commercial expansion of the Digit humanoid robot business, encompassing customer deployments, and the necessary manufacturing capacity.

Agility Robotics currently has existing customer deployments with GXO Logistics and is advancing manufacturing operations alongside its product roadmap for Digit five targeting commercial markets in logistics and manufacturing.
This development signals further investment and tangible progression in the commercialization of humanoid robotics technology.

From CMU Robotics Institute, Inside CMU’s Robotics Innovation Center reports on the establishment of a new center in Pittsburgh's Hazelwood neighborhood, reflecting the university's history and commitment to innovation.
The center encompasses 150,000 square feet and is situated along the Monongahela River.

This facility represents an extension of Carnegie Mellon University’s long-standing expertise in robotics and a dedication to advancing technological development through focused research and development.
The center's development signals a significant investment in fostering the next generation of robotic systems and related technologies within the Pittsburgh area.
This initiative provides a dedicated physical space for advanced research and collaborative projects in the field.
The expansion underscores a continued focus on pushing the boundaries of robotic capabilities.
This development indicates continued growth in applied robotics research within the region.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, YMBot D!".

This report details the introduction of the YMBot D, a foldable, wheeled humanoid robot developed by Jiangsu Yunmu Intelligent Manufacturing Technology Co., Ltd., demonstrating a convergence of mobility and object handling for industrial applications.
The robot measures one hundred sixty-five centimeters in height and weighs one hundred kilograms, incorporating twenty-two degrees of freedom and two articulated arms.
It is equipped with a mobile base enabling navigation and dexterous hands designed for tasks such as obstacle avoidance, sorting goods, and product assembly.
The system utilizes an Intel 12th generation CPU and is listed as in production with a manufacturing cost of thirty-five thousand United States dollars.
This development signifies a progression in humanoid robotics integrating advanced locomotion with precise manipulation capabilities for manufacturing environments.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Jingchu Elf!".
This report details the development and specifications of the Jingchu Elf, a wheeled service humanoid robot.
The robot stands one hundred sixty-five centimeters tall and integrates a humanoid upper body with a two-wheeled base.
The system utilizes LiDAR and depth sensing for autonomous obstacle avoidance and the capability to sort goods.
Powering the unit is an NVIDIA Ampere GPU, and the current skill score is two out of ten, reflecting early-stage capability in navigation and manipulation.
This platform is currently listed as a prototype with a research and exploratory service price of twenty-five thousand US dollars.
The development represents an advancement in mobile robotics integration and sensing technology.
Further development in navigation and manipulation algorithms is anticipated in the near future.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Max!".

This report details the development of Max, Meta's first humanoid robot prototype developed with Fourier for home assistance research, which demonstrates capabilities in movement and household object manipulation.
The prototype stands at one hundred fifty centimeters and weighs forty-eight kilograms, featuring a humanoid form, five-fingered hands, and a face screen.
Documented capabilities include obstacle avoidance, stair walking, and the operation of a dishwasher, linking physical movement with the manipulation of household objects.
The robot's skill score is three out of ten, positioning it within the developing category for general-purpose robots, serving as a platform for researching physical systems for home assistance.
This development indicates ongoing research into integrating physical skills into domestic robotic systems.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, YMBOT E3!".

This report details the introduction of the YMBOT E3, a modular bipedal humanoid robot developed for robotics education and research, which demonstrates capabilities in obstacle avoidance and goods sorting.
The YMBOT E3 stands at 140 centimeters and weighs 35 kilograms, incorporating an Intel i9 Central Processing Unit and compatibility with the ROS 2 control architecture.
The robot features a modular design and an articulated structure that supports ongoing research into motion control and manipulation techniques.

Experimental tasks, such as obstacle avoidance and sorting, are implemented to provide practical testing opportunities for users, positioning the system as an experimental platform rather than a finalized general-purpose robot.
This development suggests continued advancement in modular robotics and educational systems within the technology sector.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, ATOM!".
This segment details the introduction of ATOM, a humanoid robot designed for indoor environments with preliminary capabilities in obstacle avoidance and sorting.
The robot measures one hundred sixty centimeters and weighs fifty kilograms, featuring thirty-one degrees of freedom and electric joint actuators.
Its exterior is covered in fabric to facilitate quiet operation within homes and offices.
ATOM incorporates large language model capabilities and is currently categorized as a prototype with a listed price of twenty-five thousand dollars.
Deliveries for this robot are projected to commence by the end of two thousand twenty-six.
This development indicates progression in the integration of physical robotics and advanced language processing into domestic automation systems.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, YMBot H!".

This report details the introduction of YMBot H, a wheeled, humanoid service robot developed by Jiangsu Yunmu Intelligent Manufacturing Technology Co., Ltd., which is positioned as a preliminary service platform emphasizing mobile humanoid form over advanced physical task performance.
The robot is designed for visitor engagement in public spaces, featuring a humanlike appearance, dual arms, and a mobile base.
It measures 170 centimeters in height and weighs 75 kilograms, capable of moving at a maximum speed of 5.4 kilometers per hour and operating for a six-hour runtime.
The robot has confirmed capability in obstacle avoidance for navigation within indoor environments, although its skill scores for human guidance and manipulation remain very low.
This development indicates a focus on mobile interaction systems within the robotics sector.
From NVIDIA Developer Blog, "Build World Models for Interactive Simulation with NVIDIA Cosmos"
details the provision of world foundation models and tools to address sensor adaptation and reliable deployment challenges in physical AI.
The Cosmos Framework offers modular tools for training, optimization, and inference across various models.
Simulation recipes enable the generation of synchronized video and LiDAR data for applications such as autonomous vehicles and robotics.
Furthermore, Cosmos NIM microservices accelerate inference through techniques including quantization and speculative decoding implemented on GPUs.
Developers can utilize this framework to train models, perform reinforcement learning, and deploy optimized models employing specialized skills.
This advancement establishes a foundation for more realistic and deployable physical AI systems.
From Humanoids Daily, "New Figure 03 Robots Walk Out of BotQ in Brett Adcock’s Latest Video".
This report details footage of newly manufactured Figure 03 humanoids exiting the BotQ facility and moving across the campus.
The 19-second clip captures the robots advancing toward a parking-lot crossing, providing a visual indication of the growing robot fleet operating outside the manufacturing environment.
This video offers a brief observation of the physical progression of the robots following their production within the factory setting.
The increased number of these robots reportedly supports internal research and development initiatives for the company.
This development signals ongoing activity in the humanoid robotics sector.
And that's all the circuits for today from your Robotics Digest.
May your algorithms be elegant and your code compile smoothly!
Until tomorrow, keep building brilliantly.
